blocks.text: Every grain of rice, every tuber of yam and every kilogram of beef sold in a Nigerian market can be traced back to sunlight captured by a green leaf. Photosynthesis is the only doorway through which energy enters almost every food chain on Earth.

blocks.markdown:
## The overall reaction

Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants use light energy trapped by chlorophyll to build carbohydrate from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen as a by-product.

In words:

carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (in the presence of light and chlorophyll)

blocks.caption: The balanced equation for photosynthesis — check that carbon, hydrogen and oxygen all balance

items: Raw materials: carbon dioxide (from the air through the stomata) and water (from the soil through the roots and xylem).
Necessary conditions: light energy, chlorophyll, and a suitable temperature for the enzymes involved.
Products: glucose, which is quickly converted to starch for storage, and oxygen, which diffuses out of the leaf.
Site: the chloroplasts, mainly in the palisade mesophyll cells near the upper surface of the leaf.

blocks.title: Limiting factor
blocks.text: The factor in shortest supply, which therefore sets the rate of photosynthesis. On a bright day in a closed greenhouse, carbon dioxide is usually limiting; at dawn or under a canopy, light is limiting; on a cold morning, temperature is limiting.

blocks.markdown:
### How a leaf is built for the job

The leaf is a photosynthetic factory, and each feature has a purpose.

It is **broad and flat**, giving a large surface area to intercept light, and **thin**, so that carbon dioxide has only a short distance to diffuse. The upper surface carries a transparent **waxy cuticle** that reduces water loss without blocking light. Immediately below lies the **palisade mesophyll**, a layer of long cells packed with chloroplasts and positioned to catch light first. Beneath that, the **spongy mesophyll** has large air spaces that let gases circulate freely to every cell. **Stomata**, mostly on the lower surface, open and close to admit carbon dioxide while limiting water loss, and a network of **veins** brings water and carries away the manufactured sugar.

### The two stages

**Light stage (light-dependent, in the grana of the chloroplast)**

Chlorophyll absorbs light. The energy splits water into hydrogen and oxygen — this is **photolysis**. The oxygen is released as a by-product and the hydrogen is held by a carrier. Some energy is stored as ATP. Light is essential here.

**Dark stage (light-independent, in the stroma)**

The hydrogen and the ATP from the light stage are used to reduce carbon dioxide to carbohydrate. This series of enzyme-controlled steps is the Calvin cycle. It does not need light directly, but it stops soon after the light stage stops because it runs out of hydrogen and ATP.

blocks.title: Testing whether light is necessary for photosynthesis
blocks.prompt: Design and explain an experiment to show that light is necessary for the manufacture of starch in a leaf.

steps.text: Destarch the plant first. Keep it in complete darkness for 48 hours so that all existing starch is used up. Without this step any starch you find later might have been there from before.

Set up the variable. Cover part of one attached leaf on both surfaces with black paper or a cork stencil, leaving the rest exposed. The covered and uncovered parts of the same leaf differ only in light received.
Expose the plant to bright sunlight for several hours so photosynthesis can occur in the uncovered part.

Prepare the leaf for testing. Detach it, boil in water for one minute to kill the cells and burst the starch grains, then boil in ethanol in a water bath to remove the chlorophyll, and finally dip in warm water to soften the brittle leaf.
Test with iodine solution and read the result. The part that was exposed to light turns blue-black, showing starch is present; the covered part stays brown, showing no starch was made.
Draw the conclusion. Since light was the only difference between the two regions of the same leaf, light must be necessary for the manufacture of starch.

blocks.answer: The exposed region turns blue-black with iodine while the covered region remains brown, proving that light is necessary for photosynthesis. Note the safety point: ethanol is flammable, so heat it in a water bath and never over a direct flame.

blocks.title: Destarching, and the control
blocks.text: Two details earn marks in every practical question on this topic: destarching the plant in darkness for 48 hours beforehand, and using the covered part of the same leaf as the control. A control from a different plant would introduce other differences.

blocks.title: Do not confuse the by-product
blocks.text: Oxygen is a by-product of photosynthesis, released from the splitting of water — not from carbon dioxide. Examiners regularly ask which raw material supplies the oxygen given off, and the answer is water.

points: Photosynthesis converts carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen using light energy trapped by chlorophyll.
The raw materials are carbon dioxide and water; the necessary conditions are light, chlorophyll and a suitable temperature.
The light stage splits water in the grana; the dark stage reduces carbon dioxide to carbohydrate in the stroma.
The oxygen released comes from the photolysis of water, not from carbon dioxide.
Leaves are broad, thin, rich in chloroplasts and supplied with stomata and veins, all of which raise the efficiency of the process.
